label: L4
title: Agents II: Information, Code, Autoresearch
brief: Lecture 4 recaps the agent as a prompt in a loop: the LLM emits a structured tool request, ordinary Python routes it to an external system, wraps the result into a second prompt and calls the LLM again until it returns a final answer. Tool use is generating a reliable function call, which comes from schema enforcement learned in post-training on (instruction + schema → conforming answer) pairs; the tools are described to the model in the prompt, and task decomposition no longer needs brittle prompting. The research interlude shows what such loops can do: on six KNAPP warehouses, state-of-the-art algorithmic ideas gave about 5% over production baselines, while a coding-agent loop (propose → implement → evaluate → diagnose) raised throughput by +18.5% to +664%, and on the League of Robot Runners it went from 54 to 4,302 completed tasks, past the best entry. An autoresearch agent is the same generic loop with two tools, a persistent Python sandbox with timeouts and a scorer that grades dev predictions with a metric the agent cannot see behind, plus a prompt built from the task's description, files and metric. On MovieLens 1M (predict held-out 1–5 ratings, RMSE) the agent reached about 0.84 dev RMSE, better than SVD (0.873) and SVD++ (0.862) and close to published deep models it was not allowed to use.
kp: Agent = LLM + tools + the ability to break a task into sub-tasks and run each with the right tool; the orchestration around the LLM is ordinary Python we write.
Using a tool = generating code that calls a function, e.g. get_weather(latitude=42.3736, longitude=-71.1097); it is made reliable by schema enforcement, exactly like the complaint router.
The model learns which tools exist because we tell it in the prompt; task decomposition used to need careful, brittle prompting and is now largely built into the models.
Post-training on (instruction + schema → conforming answer) pairs, by next-word prediction, is what makes function calling reliable: the schema is part of the input.
Generic loop: reply ← model(messages, tools); no tool calls → return reply; otherwise append reply, run each call, append each result as role='tool'; give up at max_turns.
KNAPP warehouses: state-of-the-art ideas ≈ +5% over production baselines; the agentic loop (CGAR) gave +18.5% to +664% throughput across six warehouses.

Research loop: propose a hypothesis → build an experiment → measure a result you did not get to choose → add (hypothesis, result) to the state. The agent writes code, which is propose and build in one step.

Autoresearch tools: a Sandbox (persistent Python process with imports and timeouts) and a Scorer (scores dev predictions by key with the task's metric). The PROMPT and TOOLS are the only non-generic parts.
Task definition: keys, prediction-time features, train-only columns, target, metric; one table split 80/10/10 by a seeded permutation, and the split assignment is never visible to the agent.
MovieLens 1M: agent ≈ 0.84 RMSE vs k-NN 0.923, SVD 0.873, SVD++ 0.862, GLocal-K 0.822 (Torch). Protocols differ, so the comparison is rough.

topics.x: The LLM picks a tool and emits a structured request; our Python code routes it to the external system, turns the result into a second prompt and calls the LLM again until it gives a final answer. A tool call is just generated code that calls a function, made reliable by schema enforcement learned in post-training, and the available tools are described to the model in the prompt.

topics.n: The generic agent loop in code
topics.x: run_agent keeps a messages list (system prompt + goal) and, for up to max_turns, calls the chat API with TOOLS. A reply with no tool calls is the answer; otherwise the reply is appended, each call's arguments are parsed with json.loads and dispatched through TOOL_FUNCTIONS, and each result is appended as a role='tool' message carrying the tool_call_id.

On KNAPP warehouse automation, state-of-the-art algorithmic ideas gave about 5% over production baselines; a coding agent given environment, constraints, objective and a seed algorithm wrote policies as code and improved throughput by +18.5% to +664%. On Amazon Robotics' League of Robot Runners the loop went from 54 to 4,302 completed tasks, passing the best entry at commit 7.

Research is a loop: propose a hypothesis from what you know, build an experiment, measure a result you do not get to choose, and add (hypothesis, result) to the state. With an agent, the model writes code (propose + build), a sandbox runs it, a scorer measures it, and code, output and score are appended to the context.

topics.n: Instantiating autoresearch: task, sandbox, scorer, prompt
topics.x: The task is one table split 80/10/10 into train/dev/test by a seeded random permutation, described by keys, prediction-time features, train-only columns, target and metric. The sandbox is a persistent Python process whose steps time out after 180 s with variables kept; the scorer grades dev predictions and keeps the test predictions of the best attempt, so the agent never has to decide when to submit.

The agent predicts held-out ratings (1–5) from user and movie ids using only numpy, pandas, scipy and scikit-learn. Its best dev RMSE of about 0.84 beats k-NN (0.923), SVD (0.873) and SVD++ (0.862) and approaches I-AutoRec (0.831) and GLocal-K (0.822), which need Torch; evaluation protocols differ, so the comparison is approximate.

cards.f: What is an agent, per the slide definition?
cards.b: An LLM + tools (web search, calendar, Python interpreter, email, …) + the ability to break a task into sub-tasks and execute each sub-task with the right tool.
cards.x: Tools are what make it powerful; the loop around it is plain code.

cards.f: In the agent schematic, what does the LLM do and what does our code do?
cards.b: LLM: produces the request and later the final answer. Our ordinary Python: routes the request to the right external system, takes the result and builds the second prompt.
cards.x: The orchestration is not inside the model; you write it.

cards.f: What does 'using a tool' mean mechanically?
cards.b: Generating code that calls a function, e.g. search_google(“2026 FIFA World Cup final winner”) or calculate(23833 * 47374).
cards.x: The LLM writes the call; your code executes it.

cards.f: How is the tool call generated reliably?
cards.b: Schema enforcement on the LLM's response, the same mechanism as the complaint router's structured output.
cards.x: A free-text tool request would need a brittle parser.

cards.f: How does the LLM know which tools exist, and how does it learn to decompose a task?
cards.b: Tools: we describe them in the prompt. Decomposition: it used to require careful, brittle prompting; current models largely do it themselves.
cards.x: Adding a tool needs no retraining, only a description.

cards.f: Why does post-training make function calling reliable?
cards.b: Models are fine-tuned by next-word prediction on (instruction + schema → conforming answer) pairs. The schema is part of the input, so when that shape appears in context, filling it in is the continuation that scores well.
cards.x: Reliability is learned behaviour, not a parser.

cards.f: Generic agent loop: when does it stop?
cards.b: When the model's reply contains no tool calls, that reply is the answer and is returned. If max_turns is reached first, it gives up.

cards.f: In run_agent, how is a tool result fed back to the model?
cards.b: Append the model's reply to messages, run TOOL_FUNCTIONS[call.function.name](**json.loads(call.function.arguments)), then append {role: 'tool', tool_call_id: call.id, content: str(result)}.
cards.x: The request stays in the record before its result.

cards.f: KNAPP case: state of the art vs the agentic loop?
cards.b: State-of-the-art algorithmic ideas: about +5% over production baselines. Agentic loop (CGAR): +18.5% to +664% throughput across six warehouses.
cards.x: The biggest relative gains came on the weakest baselines (WAREHOUSE-03: 17.7 → 135 orders/hour).

cards.f: KNAPP: what does the user specify, and what does the coding agent iterate?
cards.b: User: environment, constraints, objective, seed algorithm. Agent: propose → implement → evaluate → diagnose, producing the policy as code.
cards.x: The output is code you can deploy, not advice.

cards.f: The research loop in four lines?
cards.b: state ← what I know; repeat: hypothesis ← propose(state); experiment ← build(hypothesis); result ← measure(experiment); state ← state + (hypothesis, result).
cards.x: The result is 'a number I did not get to choose.'

cards.f: How does the agent version of the research loop differ?
cards.b: code ← model(context) does propose and build in one step; output ← sandbox.run(code) (stdout or a traceback); score ← scorer.score(); context ← context + [code, output, score].
cards.x: The score is the measurement the agent does not control.

cards.f: In run_agent, what is not generic?
cards.b: The PROMPT and the TOOLS. For autoresearch: a Sandbox (run) and a Scorer (score) instantiated from the task, with the prompt built from the task's blurb, file table and metric.
cards.x: The loop itself is the same for every agent.

cards.f: MovieLens task spec: keys, features, train_only, target, metric?
cards.b: keys [row_id, col_id]; features [] (none at prediction time); train_only [t]; target value (rating 1–5); metric rmse(clip=(1, 5)).
cards.x: Timestamps exist in training but not at prediction time, so they cannot be features.

cards.f: What does the scorer do, and why can't the agent game it?
cards.b: It takes dev predictions by key and scores them with the metric. The agent never sees the true dev values, and the train/dev/test assignment is not in its data.
cards.x: Whenever an attempt is best so far, its test predictions are kept automatically.

cards.f: Agent RMSE on MovieLens 1M vs published methods?
cards.b: Agent ≈ 0.84 (dev set, 80/10/10). k-NN 0.923, SVD 0.873, SVD++ 0.862, ConvSVD++ 0.843, I-AutoRec 0.831, GLocal-K 0.822.
cards.x: Beats SVD/SVD++, near deep models that need Torch; protocols differ.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the three parts of an agent as defined in the lecture?
o: A separately fine-tuned copy of the LLM for each tool
An LLM
Tools such as web search, a calendar or a Python interpreter
The ability to break a task into sub-tasks and run each with the right tool
quiz.e: Agent = LLM + tools + decomposition ability. Nothing is retrained per tool: tools are described to the model in the prompt. The other three options are exactly the slide's three parts.

quiz.q: In the agent schematic, who routes the LLM's request to the appropriate external system?
o: Ordinary Python code we write
The LLM itself, inside its forward pass
The external system, which polls the LLM for work
The tokenizer
quiz.e: The slides label routing and building the second prompt as 'ours — ordinary Python'. The LLM only produces the request and the final answer, so it cannot execute anything itself.

quiz.q: Why can our routing code reliably parse the function call the LLM generates?
o: The LLM's response is schema-enforced, as with the complaint router
The LLM is always run at temperature 0
Our code uses a regex to find the bolded function name
The external system rejects malformed requests until the LLM retries
quiz.e: The slide says it plainly: schema enforcement for the LLM response, just like our router. The regex-on-bold-text approach is the brittle Lecture 3 parser that schema forcing replaced.

quiz.q: Post-training that makes function calling reliable fine-tunes on pairs of which form?
o: (instruction + schema → conforming answer), by next-word prediction
(answer → instruction), by a contrastive loss
(tool output → final answer), by RLHF only
(schema → random valid JSON), by masked-token prediction
quiz.e: The slide builds (instruction + schema → conforming answer) pairs and fine-tunes by next-word prediction; the schema sits in the input. Pairing tool outputs with answers would not teach the model to fill in a schema.

quiz.q: What does the lecture say about how an LLM learns to break a complex task into sub-tasks and pick tools?
o: It used to require careful, brittle prompting; current models largely handle it
It requires a separate planner model trained for each task
It must be hard-coded in the routing Python
It is impossible; each user request may use only one tool
quiz.e: Slide: 'This used to require careful / brittle prompting .. Not anymore.' Hard-coding the plan in the router is tempting, but the router only dispatches whatever call the model emits.

quiz.q: In the generic agent loop, when does run_agent return the model's reply as the final answer?
o: When the reply contains no tool calls
After exactly max_turns iterations
As soon as any tool returns an error
When the reply contains at least one tool call
quiz.e: 'If reply has no tool calls: return reply — it is finished.' Hitting max_turns means giving up, not answering.

quiz.q: In one turn the model replies with two tool calls. How many messages does run_agent append to `messages` in that turn?
o: 3: the reply itself plus one role='tool' message per call
2: one per tool call
1: the combined tool output
4: the reply, two results and a new user prompt
quiz.e: The code does messages.append(reply) once, then appends one {role: 'tool', tool_call_id, content} per call: 1 + 2 = 3. No new user prompt is added; the next model call simply sees the longer list.

quiz.q: KNAPP WAREHOUSE-01 went from a 487.9 orders/hour baseline to 775.3 after the agentic loop. What is the percentage improvement?
quiz.e: (775.3 − 487.9)/487.9 = 287.4/487.9 ≈ 0.589. Dividing by the final value (287.4/775.3 ≈ 37.1%) uses the wrong base; +158.9% confuses the ratio 1.589 with the gain.

quiz.q: Before the agentic loop, how much did state-of-the-art algorithmic ideas improve on KNAPP's production baselines?
o: About 5%
About 59%
Nothing; they underperformed the baselines
quiz.e: Slide: ~5% from state-of-the-art ideas. The +18.5% to +664% range is what the agentic loop achieved afterwards.

quiz.q: On the League of Robot Runners, tasks completed went from 54 at commit 0 to 3,231 at commit 7 (first past the best entry) and 4,302 at the final commit. Roughly how many times more tasks does the final commit complete than commit 0?
o: About 80×
About 60×
About 1.3×
About 8×
quiz.e: 4,302/54 ≈ 79.7. 3,231/54 ≈ 60 measures only up to commit 7, and 4,302/3,231 ≈ 1.33 compares the final commit with the best-entry crossing.

quiz.q: In the lecture's 'how research works' loop, what characterises result ← measure(experiment)?
o: It is a number the researcher does not get to choose
It is chosen to confirm the hypothesis
It replaces the whole state
It is computed once, after all experiments finish
quiz.e: The pseudocode annotates measure() as 'a number I did not get to choose'. The state is extended with (hypothesis, result), not replaced, and measurement happens every iteration.

quiz.q: Mapping the research loop onto the agent loop, which agent line does both 'propose' and 'build'?
o: code ← model(context)
output ← sandbox.run(code)
score ← scorer.score()
context ← context + [code, output, score]
quiz.e: The slide annotates code ← model(context) as 'propose and build, in one step': writing runnable code is both the hypothesis and the experiment. sandbox.run only executes it, and scorer.score is the measurement.

quiz.q: Which parts of run_agent must be specialised to build an autoresearch agent?
o: The PROMPT and the TOOLS (sandbox and scorer) instantiated from the task
The for-loop over max_turns
The check for whether the reply has tool calls
The client.chat.completions.create call
quiz.e: The loop, stopping rule and API call are generic. The general instantiation maps the task's workdir/answers/metric to the Sandbox, the Scorer and the PROMPT.

quiz.q: The MovieLens table has 997,208 rows split 80/10/10 into train/dev/test. About how many rows are in train.csv?
quiz.e: 0.8 × 997,208 ≈ 797,766, which matches the prompt's train.csv count; dev and test have 99,720 and 99,722 pairs. 897,487 would be a 90% split.

quiz.q: Why can't the agent use the timestamp t when predicting dev ratings?
o: t is train_only: it is in train.csv but not in the dev/test pairs files, so it is unavailable at prediction time
t is the target column
t encodes the train/dev/test assignment
RMSE cannot be computed with a time index present
quiz.e: The task marks t as train_only, and the prompt says it appears only in train.csv. The split assignment is a separate hidden column that the agent never sees, so t does not leak it.

quiz.q: An agent scores 7 attempts and then runs out of turns; attempt 4 had the best dev RMSE. What is its submission?
o: Attempt 4's test predictions, saved automatically when they were best so far
Nothing, because the agent never made a final submission call
Attempt 7's test predictions, the most recent
An average of all seven attempts' test predictions
quiz.e: Per the prompt, score keeps the test predictions of any attempt that is the best so far, so there is no final step to remember and nothing is lost if turns run out. 'Most recent' ignores the best-so-far rule.

quiz.q: A single run_python step runs longer than 180 seconds. What happens?
o: It is stopped and returned to the agent as a timeout; the session's variables survive
The Python session restarts and the data must be reloaded
The whole agent loop terminates
It keeps running in the background and score is called automatically
quiz.e: The prompt says long steps are stopped and handed back as a timeout, variables survive, and the agent should do less per step. The session is persistent, so nothing needs reloading.

quiz.q: Which statement about the MovieLens 1M comparison is supported by the slides?
o: The agent's ≈ 0.84 beats SVD (0.873) and SVD++ (0.862) but not GLocal-K (0.822), and protocols differ
The agent beat every published result, including GLocal-K
The agent matched I-AutoRec by using Torch
k-NN is best because its RMSE (0.923) is highest
quiz.e: Lower RMSE is better: 0.84 < 0.862 < 0.873, but 0.822 < 0.84. Torch-based deep models were not allowed for the agent, and the slide warns that protocols differ (5-fold CV vs an 80/10/10 dev set).

written.q: Write pseudocode for a generic tool-using agent loop. Then explain what you would change to turn it into an autoresearch agent, how it maps onto the research loop (propose, build, measure, update), and why the measurement must be outside the agent's control.
written.m: messages ← [system prompt, user goal]; for turn in 1..max_turns: reply ← model(messages, tools), the only LLM call; if reply has no tool calls, return reply; append reply; for each call: result ← TOOL_FUNCTIONS[name](**json.loads(args)); append {role: 'tool', tool_call_id: call.id, content: str(result)}. If the loop ends, give up. The loop is generic; an autoresearch agent changes only the PROMPT and the TOOLS: a sandbox tool (a persistent Python process with useful imports and timeouts) that runs code the model writes, and a scorer tool that grades dev predictions by key with the task's metric. Mapping: code ← model(context) is propose + build in one step; output ← sandbox.run(code) returns stdout or a traceback; score ← scorer.score() is the measurement; context ← context + [code, output, score] is the state update. The score must be 'a number I did not get to choose': the agent never sees true dev values or the train/dev/test assignment, so the only way to improve the score is to make better predictions. The scorer also keeps the best attempt's test predictions automatically, so no final submission step can be cherry-picked or forgotten.
k: Loop: initial messages, model call with tools, return when there are no tool calls, max_turns cap
Reply appended before tool results; results appended as role='tool' with the call id
PROMPT and TOOLS identified as the only non-generic parts
Sandbox (persistent, timeouts) and Scorer (dev predictions by key, metric) described
Correct mapping of propose/build/measure/update to model/sandbox/scorer/context
Independence of measurement: hidden dev labels and split; best submission saved automatically

written.q: You want an autoresearch agent to build a model for a new tabular prediction problem. Following the lecture's reference implementation, specify (a) the task-definition fields, (b) how the data are split and what the agent can and cannot see, (c) the two tools, and (d) the key prompt instructions. For each, explain how it keeps the reported score honest.
written.m: (a) keys: columns that identify a row and exist both in training and at prediction time (MovieLens: row_id, col_id); features: columns usable at prediction time (none for MovieLens); train_only: columns observed historically but unavailable when predicting (MovieLens: timestamp t); target (rating 1–5); metric (rmse with clip to [1, 5]). Separating train_only from features prevents the model from relying on information it won't have when deployed. (b) One table split 80/10/10 into train/dev/test by a seeded random permutation; the agent gets train.csv with targets and dev_pairs/test_pairs with keys only. The assignment column is never given, so the agent cannot reconstruct or exploit the split. (c) Sandbox: a persistent Python process with useful imports; a step over 180 s is stopped as a timeout but variables survive. Scorer: takes dev predictions by key, scores them with the metric, and stores the test predictions of the best attempt so far. The agent learns only through the score, never through the labels. (d) The prompt is built from the task blurb, file table and metric: each attempt writes predictions.csv and test_predictions.csv, then calls score and uses the number to decide what to try next. It should start with the simplest thing that works, change one thing at a time, and stop and report when progress stalls. Test predictions are never scored for the agent, and the best attempt is saved automatically, so the reported number reflects real held-out performance rather than a choice of when to submit.
k: All five task fields with a correct example of each, including why train_only differs from features
Seeded 80/10/10 split; hidden assignment column; agent sees only keys for dev/test
Sandbox described with persistence and timeouts
Scorer: dev-only scoring by key; best-so-far test predictions retained
Prompt guidance: simplest first, one change at a time, stop and report
Explicit argument for why each choice prevents leakage or score gaming
